Choose representations and invariants before selecting algorithms.

This family contains **17 independently navigable LeetCode topics**. Each topic has its own directory and a starting mathematical abstraction. The grouping is a learning aid, not part of LeetCode's official hierarchy.

## Topics

1. **[Array](../array/index.qmd)** — An indexed sequence with constant-time positional access.
2. **[String](../string/index.qmd)** — An ordered sequence of characters used in parsing and matching.
3. **[Hash Table](../hash-table/index.qmd)** — A key-to-slot mapping supporting expected efficient lookups.
4. **[Matrix](../matrix/index.qmd)** — A two-dimensional indexed collection used in grids and linear algebra.
5. **[Linked List](../linked-list/index.qmd)** — A sequence represented by nodes with successor references.
6. **[Doubly-Linked List](../doubly-linked-list/index.qmd)** — A linked sequence with predecessor and successor pointers.
7. **[Stack](../stack/index.qmd)** — A last-in-first-out abstract data type.
8. **[Queue](../queue/index.qmd)** — A first-in-first-out abstract data type.
9. **[Heap (Priority Queue)](../heap-priority-queue/index.qmd)** — A priority-based structure supporting efficient minimum or maximum extraction.
10. **[Ordered Set](../ordered-set/index.qmd)** — A unique-key set maintaining a comparison order.
11. **[Tree](../tree/index.qmd)** — A connected, acyclic graph supporting hierarchical reasoning.
12. **[Binary Tree](../binary-tree/index.qmd)** — A rooted tree in which each node has at most two children.
13. **[Binary Search Tree](../binary-search-tree/index.qmd)** — A binary tree governed by an ordered-key invariant.
14. **[Trie](../trie/index.qmd)** — A prefix-sharing tree for strings and sequences.
15. **[Graph Theory](../graph-theory/index.qmd)** — Vertices and edges model general relationships and connectivity.
16. **[Data Stream](../data-stream/index.qmd)** — An online sequence whose state is updated as new items arrive.
17. **[Iterator](../iterator/index.qmd)** — A stateful abstraction for visiting elements in sequence.

## Mathematical connection

A problem can carry several topic labels. Let $P$ be a problem and $\mathcal T$ the set of all tags. Its topic assignment is a set-valued mapping:

$$
L:P\longrightarrow\mathcal P(\mathcal T).
$$

Here $L(p)$ is the set of tags assigned to problem $p$. Tags describe relevant structures and techniques; they do **not** uniquely determine an algorithm or a proof of correctness.
